Chapter 4: Suffering a Verbal Loss, Reaping Real Benefits

Li Shimin wailed at the top of his lungs, Li Jiancheng’s face turned dark and gloomy, and the others looked thoroughly embarrassed.

Soon, Lady Dou rushed over in a hurry. Even Old Lady Dugu was alarmed and dispatched a trusted servant woman to inquire about the situation.

The physician retained by the Duke of Tang’s residence arrived hastily and administered several acupuncture needles to Li Xuanba, finally stopping his vomiting.

The vomit on the floor had already been cleaned up, but the stench still lingered in the air.

Li Xuanba was moved to another room. Holding a bowl of bitter medicinal broth, his face was full of world-weary melancholy.

Bitter. It really was agonizingly bitter.

He had almost set a new personal record of going a full month without drinking medicine, but now he had to keep company with decoctions once again.

The gathered adults gradually dispersed. Lady Dou went to soothe Li Jiancheng’s young companions, who had been rattled by the commotion, leaving only Li Xuanba and Li Shimin—who sat by the bedside wiping away tears—in the room.

As Li Xuanba sipped his medicine, he said in his heart to Li Shimin: *[Brother, stop crying. Your eyes are all swollen.]*

Li Shimin sniffled and muttered, "Why didn't Mother scold Eldest Brother? Mother is being partial!"

Li Xuanba sighed. How was he supposed to explain this?

The fact that Li Jiancheng had come to visit his sickbed and ended up nauseating him to the point of vomiting was truly something difficult to punish him for.

Because in this feudal era, men's personal hygiene was simply like this.

Ancient China had originally attached great importance to hygiene. As stated in the *Book of Rites*: "At the first crowing of the cock, all wash their hands and faces." Washing and grooming daily to maintain neatness had been elevated to the level of ritual propriety.

However, the stench of a hangover could not be removed merely by washing one's face and rinsing one's mouth. Moreover, at this time, there was no breath-freshening toothpaste or mouthwash—people only used green salt.

As for bathing, because people had long hair back then and no hairdryers, failing to keep warm after bathing could easily cause migraines. Thus, following so-called health cultivation lore, some people disliked bathing.

Others were simply too lazy to bathe.

Society did not hold high standards for the personal hygiene of scholar-officials.

For instance, Bai Juyi once wrote of himself, *"Not having bathed for years, dirt covers my skin."* Su Shi also wrote, *"Thinning hair barely reaching my ears, yet bathing once a month is still a hassle."*

If one argued that poets were merely expressing emotions with exaggeration, Wang Anshi's habit of "never washing soiled clothes, never washing a dirty face"—where the dirt on his face was so thick his students thought he suffered from a fatal disease and brought a famous doctor, only for the doctor to prescribe "just wash your face"—was officially recorded in the *History of Song*.

Not to mention that this period had just emerged from the Northern and Southern Dynasties, where sons of aristocratic families held the demeanor of Wei and Jin literati in high fashion; "catching lice while conversing" was considered a noble, elegant lifestyle.

The hangover stench that Li Xuanba found unbearable was, in the eyes of outsiders, the "fragrance" of a refined scholar.

Wasn't the liquor aroma fermented overnight fragrant? It even spared them the need for incense, acting as a scent of virility capable of making courtesans blush.

Therefore, when Li Jiancheng brought his friends to visit his sick younger brother while hungover, Li Xuanba really couldn't directly say that he had been vomited into sickness by their hangover stench.

Doing so would not only offend Li Jiancheng and his companions, but also be an unconventional act going against the trend of the times, drawing ridicule and condemnation from many. Those people wouldn’t care that he was just a child.

Li Xuanba didn't mind these external evaluations himself. He knew he would cling to his Second Brother in the future and become a prince, so his reputation regarding such trivial matters was completely irrelevant. However, his mother and grandmother wouldn't think so.

*[As a younger son who cannot inherit the noble title, if I am to serve as an official in the world, reputation is paramount. Since the Han Dynasty, cultivating a reputation among aristocratic children had to begin in childhood. If a bad reputation spreads when one is young, it becomes extremely difficult to turn things around when grown up.]*

*[With this body of mine, I cannot take to the battlefield to earn military merits. I can only rely on hereditary privilege or the imperial examinations. To be promoted through privilege requires recommendations; as for the imperial exams, students are recommended for admission, exams are not anonymous, and selection also considers the candidate's reputation.]*

Hearing his younger brother’s words, Li Shimin indignantly wiped his eyes with the back of his hand and said, "It is clearly their fault! Why should it damage *your* reputation?"

Li Xuanba finally finished the bitter medicine. Li Shimin took the empty bowl and popped a sugar candy into Li Xuanba’s mouth.

Li Xuanba savored the candy and continued: *[This era is simply like this.]*

Li Shimin pouted. "Even if we must act like that toward outsiders, shouldn't Mother scold Eldest Brother behind closed doors? Why did you have to apologize to him, saying it was your poor health that made him lose face?"

This was what grieved Li Shimin the most.

Ah-Xuan was clearly the one suffering, so why did Ah-Xuan have to endure his discomfort and apologize to Li Jiancheng?!

Li Xuanba asked Li Shimin for water.

Li Shimin hurriedly handed the warm water to Li Xuanba. Once Li Xuanba finished drinking, Li Shimin set the cup back on the small bedside table.

*[Mother did it for my own good. Because in the future, I will have to rely on Eldest Brother to make a living. By taking the blame voluntarily now, Mother will surely compensate me in private later. Mother treats us very well; don't resent her.]*

Second Brother was still young, and Li Xuanba hadn't originally intended to talk about these matters with him. However, although his Second Brother cried easily, he also had a hot temper. He was deeply worried that Second Brother might start clashing with Li Jiancheng prematurely because of this incident.

Second Brother was a full ten years younger than Li Jiancheng. Li Jiancheng had already secured a minor official post through hereditary privilege, whereas Second Brother was still just a child who had only recently begun his education. If Second Brother threw a fit now, it would only earn him a reputation for being unruly.

As for provoking Li Jiancheng, Li Xuanba truly felt innocent and helpless.

He really hadn't deliberately tried to trouble Li Jiancheng. On the contrary, he had even tried to curry favor with Li Jiancheng before.

Li Xuanba knew his own limits; he couldn't change the future where the brothers turned against each other in fratricide.

Given Second Brother's current age, the founding emperor of the dynastic state was bound to be the Duke of Tang, Li Yuan.

Anyone with a bit of historical common sense knew that the Xuanwu Gate Incident did not actually depend on the wills of Li Jiancheng and Li Shimin. The conflict between Li Jiancheng and Li Shimin was always a trial of strength between Li Yuan and Second Brother.

As long as Li Yuan remained emperor, Li Jiancheng and Li Shimin were doomed to fratricidal strife.

However, before that tragic brotherhood struggle, if he managed to live past the age of sixteen, sixteen-year-old Li Shimin would follow Li Yuan to battle. Frail and sickly as he was, Li Xuanba wouldn't be able to travel around, so he would definitely have to rely on Li Jiancheng, who would be guarding the rear, for a living.

By the time the Tang Dynasty was established, he would be twenty-one. That meant he would have to live at Li Jiancheng's mercy for five whole years.

To make those five years more tolerable, a pragmatic opportunist like Li Xuanba naturally tried to get a little closer to Li Jiancheng.

What he hadn't anticipated was that Li Jiancheng had originally been merely indifferent toward him. After he deliberately tried to get closer several times, Li Jiancheng actually grew somewhat disgusted with him instead.

After testing the waters a few times, Li Xuanba saw through Li Jiancheng's mindset.

It wasn't that Li Jiancheng was inherently evil.

First of all, Li Jiancheng had been an only child for ten years. Suddenly having two favored younger brothers show up, it was inevitable he felt somewhat uncomfortable.

Conflicts between firstborns and second-borns happened even in modern times.

Not to mention that he and Second Brother were not only sons born to the Duke of Tang's Residence after ten years of anticipation, but also auspicious prodigy twins. Originally, Li Jiancheng had been the center of attention for everyone in the duke's residence. Now that the spotlight had shifted to himself and Second Brother, anyone would feel awkward for a while.

Secondly, Li Jiancheng was a full ten years older than him.

In modern terms, it was like a sixteen-year-old high school student being pestered by a six-year-old preschooler—he was bound to be written all over with the word "annoyed." The more Li Xuanba clung to him, the more annoyed he became.

Furthermore, he and Second Brother were overly intelligent. They wouldn't just look up with worshipful faces and shout, "Eldest Brother is so amazing!" whenever Li Jiancheng said something casually; instead, they would look at him with puzzled faces that said, "That's it?"

Precocious little kids were even more annoying. Who had the patience to coax children?! Annoying to death!!

If he and Second Brother were even younger, say around Fourth Brother's current age, they might have gotten along better with Li Jiancheng.

Combining the above reasons, Li Jiancheng treated the two-year-old Li Yuanji pretty well, maintained a mediocre attitude toward Li Shimin (who didn't care to pay attention to him), and somewhat disliked Li Xuanba, who was always bothering him.

Besides that, as the eldest son of the legitimate line, following the customs of prominent families, Li Jiancheng was raised by their grandmother, whose health was still robust back then. He and Second Brother, on the other hand, were closer to their mother.

Whenever conflicts arose between grandmother and mother, Li Xuanba, taking advantage of being young and sickly—knowing grandmother wouldn't get angry at him—often took his mother's side. Li Jiancheng probably thought he wasn't filial enough toward their grandmother and couldn't stand the sight of it.

Combined, Li Jiancheng disliked him, this "bratty kid," even more.

However, such minor friction would fade away under the wash of interests and rationality once they grew older.

During the Wei and Jin dynasties, China re-entered aristocratic politics. Apart from the imperial family, where brothers frequently fought amongst themselves, the status of the eldest legitimate son in ordinary noble clans was unshakeable.

This was not the "legitimate versus concubine-born distinction" hyped up by modern marketing accounts.

The concept of "legitimate vs. concubine-born" in backyard drama webnovels borrowed from Korean and European tropes, where a child's status strictly followed the mother's status. In China, however, the father was paramount. As long as a child was entered into the genealogy, apart from the supreme status of the eldest legitimate son, the difference in status among the other sons was minimal. Compared to concubine-born sons, a legitimate younger son might at most get a bit more family property, while the political resources invested in them by the family were actually quite similar.

Only after the Song Dynasty, when becoming an official relied mainly on imperial examinations, did the gap between the eldest legitimate son and other children narrow.

Under the current social conditions, the imperial examinations had only just emerged, and very few entered officialdom through them; the court was still dominated by aristocratic politics. As the eldest legitimate son who could inherit the noble title, Li Jiancheng's status was naturally far higher than that of his younger brothers, who had to carve out their own paths.

Thus, at this time, "legitimate vs. secondary" meant the eldest legitimate son was considered "legitimate," while all other sons, including brothers born of the same mother, were categorized as "secondary branches."

No matter how many younger brothers Li Jiancheng had, none of them posed any threat to his position.

Furthermore, according to "filial piety," children could not divide the household while their parents were alive. No matter how capable the younger brothers were, they had to obediently live under Li Jiancheng's roof. Even after marrying and establishing careers, they would merely be the "Second Branch," "Third Branch," or "Such-and-Such Branch" of the Duke of Tang's Residence. The more capable they were, the greater help they would be to Li Jiancheng.

In summary, to put it bluntly: no matter how poorly Li Jiancheng treated him now, once Li Xuanba grew up, he would still have to dutifully seek out his eldest brother to repair their relationship; otherwise, his future life would not be pleasant.

Even if Lady Dou and Old Lady Dugu knew that Li Xuanba's illness was caused by Li Jiancheng's mistake, they couldn't punish Li Jiancheng over such a minor matter. Otherwise, the one suffering the consequences in the future would be Li Xuanba.

After all, only Li Xuanba himself knew that his future status would not rely on Li Jiancheng, but on his Second Brother who would become emperor.

Li Xuanba picked out some simpler aspects of his predicament and the distinction between the primary heir and other sons to explain to Li Shimin, preventing Li Shimin from going to trouble Li Jiancheng.

Causing trouble would only lead to a greater loss later. It was better to swallow this grievance, win some heartache and sympathy from their mother and grandmother, and ask for tangible benefits.

"So complicated." Li Shimin pushed Li Xuanba inward a bit, kicked off his shoes, and squeezed onto the bed to lie side-by-side with Li Xuanba.

Li Xuanba: *[You don't understand?]*

Li Shimin: "Ah-Xuan means that in the future, you have to rely on him to live, so you can't offend him."

Li Xuanba: *[That's pretty much it.]*

Li Shimin turned his head to look at his younger brother. On his chubby face, which still retained its baby fat, was a serious expression rarely seen on a child. "My health is good. I will go perform distinguished service and earn a new noble title of my own! As long as I am granted a title, we can divide the household early without violating filial piety!"

Li Xuanba: *[Huh?]*

Li Shimin said earnestly, "Once I get a title, I will take Ah-Xuan away. Your brother will support you! We won't rely on Li Jiancheng to raise us. You don't have to curry favor with him."

Li Xuanba froze for a moment, then broke into a chuckle. "Alright."

Li Shimin's smile returned as he held out his hand. "Come, your brother will high-five you as a vow! I will definitely achieve military merit and take you away as quickly as possible."

He paused, then added, "And we'll take Mother with us, too!"

"Pfft..." Li Xuanba laughed. "Alright."

"Ah, I'm sleepy. Move over a bit more." Li Shimin pushed Li Xuanba further toward the inside of the bed and spread himself out carelessly into a star shape. "Good afternoon, Ah-Xuan."

Li Xuanba muttered, "We just woke up not too long ago..."

Though he said that, he was feeling a bit sleepy himself.

Head to head, the two children quickly fell asleep in the gentle breeze drifting in through the courtyard window.

Standing by the window, Lady Dou wiped her tears continuously.

She knew the telepathic connection between Third Son and Second Son was even more extraordinary than outsiders imagined.

Third Son could "speak" to Second Son without opening his mouth. Although Second Son could hear Third Son's inner voice, he couldn't speak in his mind like Third Son did. Thus, when the two children conversed, it often looked like Second Son was "talking to himself."

Though Lady Dou couldn't hear what Third Son said to Second Son, she could guess most of it from Second Son's responses.

"Second Brother and Third Brother are far too mature for their age," Lady Li sighed as she wiped away Lady Dou's tears.

She had originally been behind closed doors working on embroidery for her future in-laws for her wedding next year. Upon hearing that trouble had occurred with her younger brother, she rushed over to help her mother.

It just so happened that among the people fooling around with Li Jiancheng was her future husband, Chai Shao. She needed to warn Chai Shao not to go spreading rumors about the Duke of Tang's household.

As a daughter raised under Lady Dou's care, and with Li Xuanba being an obedient, thoughtful child who often brought Li Shimin to play with her, Lady Li naturally shared a deeper bond with Li Shimin and Li Xuanba.

Overhearing their conversation, Lady Li naturally favored her two younger brothers and felt quite distressed.

She couldn't help but mutter, "How old is Li Jiancheng already? Why is he still throwing fits like a child? Doesn't he know Third Brother is frail? Bringing a bunch of outsiders reeking of alcohol to visit a sickbed—does that look like visiting the sick at all?"

"San-niang, quiet!" Lady Dou said sternly.

Lady Li sighed. "Yes, yes, yes. After I marry, I'll still need support from my maiden family, so I have to cater to him, the future Duke of Tang."

She felt extremely suffocated inside.

Since childhood, Lady Li had brandished swords, wielded spears, read books, and written essays, believing she was no different from a man.

Only when she was about to be married did she realize the world of difference between women and men.

Her mother, who used to dote on her and indulge her, confiscated her weapons, ink, and brushes, forcing her to undergo intensive training in embroidery, household management, and... serving others and enduring hardship.

No matter how cherished a daughter was in her own family, things changed once she married.

No matter how good her in-laws were, they would never be as warm and caring as her own parents. She was not marrying out of mutual love for Chai Shao; rather, it was the Duke of Tang's daughter marrying into the family of the Duke of Julu Commandery. There were far too many matters she had to be mindful of.

"I will add more to your dowry. You are more capable than your mother; Chai Shao is a considerate person, and his mother is also kind-hearted. You will surely live a better life than I have." Lady Dou gently patted the back of her daughter's hand, tucking away the weakness on her face. "After you marry... if you have spare capacity, provided that you yourself are living well, lend a helping hand to Third Brother."

Lady Li smiled and said, "Brothers from my maiden family are my backing. Even if Mother didn't say so, I would still do it."

What's more, among her brothers, Third Brother was the best to her. When she was confined to her courtyard doing embroidery, Third Brother would often secretly send military treatises and geographical records to relieve her boredom.

Although she had no chance of fulfilling her childhood dream of becoming a great general in this lifetime, being able to read those books and dream a little longer was nice enough.

Lady Dou nodded. "However, your own well-being comes first. If you aren't living well and yet try to help Third Brother, knowing that child's temperament, he won't accept it."

Lady Li covered her mouth. "I know, I know. Rest assured, Mother, I will definitely live well. Shall we go inside to see them again?"

Lady Dou hesitated for a moment, then sighed, "Let us not disturb their afternoon nap."

"Sleeping right after waking up—two little piglets," Lady Li teased in a low voice, supporting her tired mother as they departed. "Oh right, Mother, a while ago Third Brother mentioned he wanted to take a shop to practice managing things. Mother said he was too young and would give him one in a few years. In my view, although he is young, he calculates accounts clearly. Why not give it to him now so he has more pocket money and feels a bit happier?"

Lady Dou hesitated briefly, then sighed, "You are right."

The entire Duke of Tang's Residence belonged to her eldest son. Aside from the dowry set aside for her daughter, she had better leave more of her private savings to her other children.

Lady Dou suddenly remembered her fourth son, and her heart twinged with pain.

Disgust, guilt, avoidance, and anger intertwined within her, causing her brows to knit tightly.

"Accompany Mother to see Fourth Son as well," Lady Dou said in a low voice.

Lady Li's expression instantly fell. "Ah, alright."

Lady Dou lightly squeezed the hand her daughter used to support her and said, "Fourth Son is still a child. It's normal for him to be a bit naughty now; he'll improve as he grows older."

Lady Li: "Oh, heh."

Lady Li rolled her eyes in her mind.

*Improve when he grows older? He still needs to be educated! With Fourth Brother being doted on like this, he'll probably only get worse in the future.*

*Grandmother clearly no longer has the energy to raise children, yet she refuses to give Fourth Brother back to Mother. Who knows what Fourth Brother will turn into in the future.*

Noticing what Lady Li was thinking, Lady Dou said, "The fault lies with me, not Fourth Son or Mother."

If she hadn't suffered from hysteria when giving birth, Mother wouldn't have forbidden her from raising Fourth Son.

Lady Li said, "Alright, Mother, if you stall any longer, you won't have time to see Fourth Brother. I reckon Grandmother is about to summon you to attend to her illness again. Let's go quickly!"

She tugged Lady Dou along, quickening her pace.

"Sigh, slow down. Why are you as impatient as Second Brother?" Lady Dou said helplessly.

Lady Li chuckled, "What do you mean I'm like Second Brother? I'm older than him—it's Second Brother who takes after me!"

Lady Dou laughed, "Fine, fine, Second Brother takes after you."

The soundly sleeping Second Young Master Li: "Achoo... mm... zzz..."

Beside him, Third Young Master Li curled into a ball, instinctively extending his limbs even in deep sleep to refuse being used as a cooling bolster by his older brother.

...

"Third Son is a sensible child," Old Lady Dugu remarked slowly upon learning how Li Xuanba had taken all the blame upon himself. "Harmony at home brings prosperity to all. Eldest Son will inherit the title of Duke of Tang in the future and is the pillar of this household. Third Son ought to show some deference."

Madame Zhang was one of the dowry maids brought by Old Lady Dugu. She had never married, binding her hair up to become a senior maidservant, and was Old Lady Dugu's most trusted confidante.

As Nanny Zhang massaged Old Lady Dugu's legs, which had grown stiff from lying down too long, she sighed, "It's just that Third Young Master is only six years old. Being so precocious is truly heartbreaking."

Old Lady Dugu let out a long sigh and said, "Eldest Son has only just gotten engaged; he is still a child himself, with a somewhat immature temperament. Once he marries and has children of his own, he will understand how to show consideration for his younger brothers."

Nanny Zhang replied, "Of course. Eldest Young Master is most benevolent; he was merely a bit rash in his actions and didn't think things through, which led to outsiders offending Third Young Master."

Old Lady Dugu said, "Indeed. Those people were truly shameless as well. Eldest Son invited them along to visit his younger brother merely out of politeness; how could they actually come along? Did their families never teach them etiquette for visiting the sick? Especially that Chai Shao—he doesn't look like a good person to me at all!"

Old Lady Dugu deeply disliked this prospective grandson-in-law chosen by Lady Dou. Old Lady Dugu was the elder sister of the late Empress Wenxian, Dugu Jialuo. She had originally wanted to marry her granddaughter to her sister's grandson, Yang Jian, the current emperor's second son, cementing their familial ties even further.

Although Yang Jian was not yet created a prince, he and the Crown Prince were both sons born of the Empress, so being named a prince was only a matter of time. Yang Jian's first wife had passed away early, leaving his inner household without a mistress. With San-niang's background, her position as Yang Jian's successor wife would be solid, making her a Prince's Consort in the future!

Furthermore, the Crown Prince seemed to be in poor health. If the Crown Prince died young and Yang Jian became the Crown Prince, San-niang would become the Crown Princess and eventually the Empress!

Yet Lady Dou refused to take such a grand path to nobility and even persuaded her son.

What was a Commandery Duke? How could it compare to being a Prince's Consort?

Thinking about how her son had actually opposed her decision for Lady Dou's sake made Old Lady Dugu feel deeply aggrieved.

Knowing Old Lady Dugu detested Chai Shao, Nanny Zhang casually criticized Chai Shao as well, pushing the responsibility of today's incident onto him, making it sound as though Chai Shao had instigated Li Jiancheng to act this way.

After hurling a few curses, Old Lady Dugu's anger finally subsided.

As for Li Shimin and Li Jiancheng, Old Lady Dugu naturally held affection for her grandsons in her heart.

Thinking of Li Xuanba's frail physique and how hard it would be for him to achieve success on his own in the future, Old Lady Dugu felt immense heartache for him.

Under Nanny Zhang's subtle prompting, Old Lady Dugu made the exact same decision as Lady Dou.

"Didn't Third Son want to take a shop to play around with? Since he likes reading books, let's give him a bookstore first," Old Lady Dugu decided. "Eldest Son will be a capable man in the future and won't look down on my meager dowry savings. Giving a bit more private property to Third Son is something Eldest Son can understand."

Nanny Zhang said, "Eldest Young Master has lofty ambitions; he certainly won't quibble over such things."

Old Lady Dugu smiled, "Naturally."

Seeing her goal achieved, Nanny Zhang felt delighted inside.

The image of Third Young Master smiling and saying to her, "Thank you, Nanny Zhang, for the clothes you embroidered," flashed through her mind.

As Old Lady Dugu's confidante, all the young masters and young ladies in the residence were very polite and respectful to Nanny Zhang.

However, only this sentence from Third Young Master Li truly entered her heart.

All the embroidery gifted by Old Lady Dugu to her grandchildren came from Nanny Zhang's hands. Everyone else thanked Old Lady Dugu, but Third Young Master alone expressed extra gratitude to her.

Ever since then, whenever she sent embroidery to Third Young Master, it felt like more than just a grandmother giving gifts to a grandson—it was as if she, too, had gained a grandson of her own.

Even though she knew it was merely an illusion, the lonely Nanny Zhang still cared all the more for Third Young Master Li.

If not for Nanny Zhang helping behind the scenes, it wouldn't have been so easy for Third Young Master Li to feign illness time and again just to keep Lady Dou resting by his side.

...

When Li Xuanba woke up, two shops had been added under his name: one selling rouge and cosmetics, and the other selling books.

Li Shimin said with an air of mock maturity, "Is this what Ah-Xuan meant by taking a loss with Eldest Brother so Mother and Grandmother would compensate you in private? Pretty nice! Ah-Xuan, go provoke Eldest Brother once more, and then I can just rely on you to support me!"

"Get lost!" Li Xuanba kicked Li Shimin.

*Just moments ago you said you were going to achieve military merits and support me yourself! Where is your ambition! How did it turn into me supporting you!*

chunks.chapterTitle: 第5章 一唱一和降掌柜
chunks.chineseText:
第5章 一唱一和降掌柜

唐国公府的公子都是在五周岁开始启蒙，学习识字断句和算术。
　　启蒙后，他们就能每个月领零花钱了。
　　李玄霸算了算他和二哥每个月能攒下来的零花钱，当时就想做点小本生意。
　　自己不能建功立业，如果能趁着隋朝还没乱起来攒点家产，跟着李建成讨生活的时候，就算李建成不待见自己，自己也能用钱买命。
　　原本李玄霸以为小本生意有唐国公府这个靠山，沿路支个摊子就能做。
　　一番调研后，他才发现自己身为专门逮着李世民薅毛的历史营销号小编，对隋唐的了解还不够。
　　啊？历史营销号本来就是史盲骗史盲？那没事了，自己的业务能力没问题。
　　隋唐的商业制度是怎样运作的？
　　隋文帝新建大兴城，推行坊市制度，控制人口流动，抑制商业活动。
　　“坊”是居民区，“市”是交易区。隋文帝取消所有沿街商铺，坊内和连接坊的道路两侧不允许有任何商业活动，所有市场交易必须在大兴城的东西二市进行。
　　“坊市”门禁管理非常严格。比如市的交易时间，“凡市以日午，击鼓三百声而众以会；日入前七刻，击钲三百声而众以散”，只开放一个下午。
　　这一套规矩下放到全国所有大小城池，且“诸非州县之所，不得置市”。
　　隋唐之初，这个规矩十分严苛。如果按照他之前的想法，私自拖个小推车出去贩卖东西，轻则杖六十，重则贩卖者和购买者都以盗窃罪论处。
　　那么可以做生意的市有多大呢？
　　隋唐的坊市数量是以城市行政等级划分，不看人口数量。都城大兴城和东都洛阳城的坊市数量都是在一百至一百一十之间，而市只有两个。
　　所以市中的店铺已经不能叫寸土寸金，只能叫有市无价，早在隋文帝开国之初就被勋贵瓜分干净了。
　　如果李玄霸想要在坊里偷偷做生意，得等到贞观，他哥见这样严格控制商业活动实在是不方便，稍稍放宽了对坊内商业的控制，才能在有背景保护的前提下，支个摊子卖东西。
　　如果他想随意在路边找个屋子当商铺彻夜卖东西，就只能等安史之乱后，坊市制度彻底崩塌了。
　　李玄霸问了娘亲一声，能不能在唐国公府的自家店铺中寄卖东西，得到否认的回答后，他就放弃了做生意的打算。
　　平民穿越到初唐盛唐，支个摊子做小本生意创业发家是不可能的，就连他这个唐国公府三公子都做不到，唉。
　　没想到，只是替大兄背个过错，居然能拿到两间铺子？
　　虽然李玄霸骂自家哥没志气，但那时他的想法也是，真香！
　　如果不是之后还要跟着李建成讨生活，不能把李建成得罪狠了，他都想去主动碰瓷了。
　　大兴城和后来的长安城一样，皇帝行宫和达官贵人的官邸都在东市“都会市”附近。东市多做珠宝、古董、高档布料之类的奢侈品买卖，街道也比西市宽敞。
　　西市“利人市”是普通人的集市。除了囊括所有日常用品，当贞观丝绸之路重新开启后，胡人都聚集在西市。到了盛唐，西市的繁华会超过东市。
　　现在西市虽然还没有胡商加成，因商贾如果没有背靠勋贵没有资格去东市，所以已经形成了“东市贵、西市富”的雏形。
　　无论东市还是西市的店铺，都早就被勋贵瓜分完毕。隋朝才过了一代皇帝，勋贵远没到洗牌到需要卖铺子的程度。
　　窦氏和独孤老夫人能拿出铺子给六岁孩童“玩耍”，可见她们二人嫁妆之丰厚，窦氏和独孤氏在隋朝权势之高。
　　李玄霸在外人面前是个沉默寡言的形象，但他在李世民这里是个“话痨”，心里从出门起就叭叭叭个不停。
　　李世民趴在马车车窗上，一边好奇地东张西望，一边频频点头，告诉李玄霸他在听。
　　李玄霸把隋朝的坊市制度一一讲解给他哥听后，又说起了他从祖母和娘亲的嫁妆看出的“内情”。
　　祖母嫁妆中的店铺多在东市。不过那其实不算祖母的嫁妆，而是文献皇后给祖母的赏赐。
　　母亲嫁妆中的店铺多在西市。从这件事可以看出，隋文帝杀光宇文氏直系男丁后虽然没对北周的公主动手，但也有稍稍压制襄阳长公主一家。
　　李世民转头：“是这样吗？但祖母给你的铺子在西市，母亲给你的铺子在东市啊。”
　　李玄霸：【所以虽然祖母和母亲都疼爱我们，疼爱程度还是不同的。】
　　李世民继续看向马车车窗外，下巴搁在交叠手臂上的小脑袋晃了晃：“阿玄，你说东市做贵人的买卖，西市做平民的买卖。那书本字画之类的店铺，是不是东市更多？”
　　李玄霸：【是。国子学也在东市附近，求仕学子皆寄居东市周围坊中。】
　　国子学即国子监。隋炀帝大业三年改名国子监，唐高祖武德元年改回国子学，唐太宗贞观元年又改成国子监。
　　李世民撇嘴：“那西市的书铺中的书能卖出去吗？”
　　李玄霸：【西市靠近佛寺。祖母给的店铺主要以卖雕版印刷的佛经为主，收益还是不错的。祖母虽不如母亲宠爱我们，但我们也是她的心尖尖。】
　　李世民坐回李玄霸身边，凑在李玄霸耳边小声道：“祖母的心尖尖一定分成了很多瓣，大兄是最大的那一瓣。”
　　李玄霸忍笑。二哥的吐槽真是犀利，放后世网络上，也一定能成为冲浪好手。
　　窦氏给李玄霸的铺子是她生意最红火的店铺之一，是她还未谈婚论嫁，在家练习管家时最先拥有的铺子。管理铺子的都是从娘家跟来的老人。
　　这间铺子的隔壁，就是窦氏给即将出嫁的女儿李三娘的嫁妆。
　　此次出游，窦氏要伺候独孤老夫人腾不出手，所以是李三娘带着两个弟弟来。
　　这李三娘，就是后世李世民吐槽“比我脾气还暴躁”平阳昭公主。
　　后世因李世民赐死平阳昭公主次子，有许多阴谋论写李世民苛待平阳昭公主。
　　李玄霸就在这件事上大书特书，引来无数流量，完成了上司的绩效指标考核。
　　为了编出合格的谣言，李玄霸首先要查到真实的资料，才能九真一假，令人信服。所以他知道事实不是如此。
　　首先，平阳昭公主在武德元年就被解除了所有兵权，一直住在长安。
　　“娘子关”之名在平阳昭公主出生几百年前就有这个名字，是后人牵强附会。
　　平阳昭公主自唐朝建立后就被夺走兵权，一直住在长安，没有镇守过娘子关，自然也不可能和当时主要带兵的秦王李世民有冲突。
　　再者，李世民其实有厚待平阳昭公主。只是封建时代对女性的厚待，不符合现代人的思想而已。
　　在柴令武与巴陵公主卷入谋反前，柴绍长子袭爵谯国公，次子因娶了公主册封襄阳郡公，是当时难得的一门双公顶级勋贵家族。
　　后来柴绍长子柴哲威虽被坐罪迁岭南，但很快就起复为交州都督，在李世民去世后的第二年死在任职上。
　　都督是地方最高军事长官。贞观年间撤内地都督，剩下的每一个都督都是手握重兵的封疆大吏。可见李世民对他的信任。
　　李世民还厚待平阳昭公主的老下属，比如柴家家僮马三宝。
　　李渊起兵反隋，柴绍与平阳昭公主分开行动，柴绍独自跑到太原，平阳昭公主招兵起义，马三宝随侍平阳昭公主左右，是平阳昭公主的心腹。
　　贞观元年，家奴出身的马三宝被李世民晋为国公。贞观三年去世时，谥号为“忠”。
　　还有平阳昭公主的丈夫柴绍，名列凌烟阁二十四功臣第十四名，在程咬金、侯君集、李勣之前。
　　柴绍有击破吐谷浑、突厥和平叛的战功，但比起凌烟阁其他将领来说，显然有些失色。他名列凌烟阁位次这么高，后世公认“关系户”。
　　至于为什么不直接嘉赏平阳昭公主本人，也不公开提平阳昭公主的战功，这就是封建时代的局限性。
　　封建时代封赏女子基本都只封赏其男性家眷。李世民超规格厚待平阳昭公主的丈夫、儿子、心腹，就是厚待平阳昭公主了。
　　其实唐朝女性地位虽然较宋以后高，但也没高到哪里去。唐初女子出门时，必须佩戴遮盖全身的羃离。到唐高宗李治时，因为民间女子流行起只遮掩住颈部的帷帽，还专门下诏训斥过。
　　所以平阳昭公主抛头露面招兵买马当女将军一事，在当时很是离经叛道。
　　从唐初开始，从李渊到主流士人，都致力于抹消平阳昭公主身为女将军的事迹。
　　李渊曾刚建立唐朝，就让温大雅给他写了《大唐创业起居注》歌功颂德。在此书中，平阳昭公主所有事迹全部被抹去，变成了李渊高瞻远瞩，智勇双全，连平阳昭公主参与攻破长安的战功都分润给了儿子和心腹。
　　李渊自己发布的《褒授岐平定等诏》中，也只字未提平阳昭公主。
　　李渊能给平阳昭公主谥号，并以鼓吹之礼下葬，已经是额外奖赏。
　　《旧唐书》问世之前，平阳昭公主的光芒十分黯淡。
　　在这样的社会背景下，尉迟乙僧绘制了一副平阳昭公主据鞍佩櫜鞬的将军画像。
　　此画是在贞观年间，尉迟乙僧给李世民当宿卫官时绘制。他能获得绘制公主画像的许可，还找到对当年公主戎马生涯有记忆的人取材，背后故事不用多说了。
　　李世民也理应怀念这位女将军，厚待她的丈夫和后人。
　　因为根据历史上的蛛丝马迹，平阳昭公主的兵都交予了李世民，后来全成了李世民的死忠。
　　这些人一到李世民麾下就忠心耿耿，总不能是因为李世民自带魅惑能力，引人纳头就拜。
　　或许应当是应了后世人那句评价，平阳昭公主“盖难弟矣”。
　　李玄霸认为，平阳昭公主就算被夺了兵权，曾经麾下将领也会给她几分薄面。她居住在长安时，李渊和李建成应当都会捧着这个没有威胁，但有声望的将军公主。
　　所以他早早地扑上去抱大腿，以求唐朝建立，二哥李世民在外打仗护不住他时，自己如果不讨李渊和李建成的喜欢，能有个人保护自己。
　　逼急了他就不要脸地往姐姐家一住，说不定还能救姐姐一命。
　　姐姐的死因虽然史书上没有记载，但其次子柴令武年龄应该与其妻巴陵公主相仿，其出生时间正好与姐姐辞世的时间接近。所以姐姐死因很可能是难产，或者高龄产子后留下的并发症。
　　有他不要脸地住在公主府打扰姐姐和姐夫小两口亲近，说不准柴令武就不会出生，姐姐就不会死了。
　　双赢！
　　虽然李玄霸的刻意亲近在李建成那里起了反效果，但在三姐这里效果拔群。
　　女子待字闺中，李渊没给女儿取小名，平阳昭公主现在在家里和外面只称“李三娘”“三娘子”。
　　李三娘比李玄霸和李世民早出门。待李玄霸和李世民下马车的时候，李三娘已经戴着遮掩全身的冪离，在店铺门口等着了。
　　“二郎，三郎！”性格风风火火的李三娘还未等马车停稳，就伸手拉开了马车门，把两个弟弟抱下来。
　　李玄霸乖巧被抱。
　　李世民使劲挣扎：“我自己走，不要抱。”
　　李玄霸很乖巧，李三娘揉了揉李玄霸的脑袋，就把弟弟放了下来。
　　李世民不乖巧，李三娘就满脸坏笑地把弟弟死命死禁锢在怀里，任由李世民怎么折腾都不放。
　　李世民对李玄霸伸手：“阿玄，救我！”
　　李玄霸不仅后退一步，还在内心嘲讽：【给阿姊当玩具是弟弟的宿命，认命吧。】
　　李世民怒道：“那你怎么不给阿姊当玩具！”
　　李三娘笑出了银铃声：“三郎说你是我的玩具？三郎哟，别说悄悄话，阿姊也想听三郎说话。”
　　李玄霸点头：“好。”
　　李世民更生气了：“我让你开口说话你不说，阿姊让你开口说话你就答应？！”
　　李玄霸点头：“对。”
　　李世民气得张牙舞爪要往弟弟身上扑，可惜被李三娘牢牢控制住，只能在半空中徒劳无用地挥舞着小短手。
　　“咳，三娘子，先进店里？”旁边一个戴着胡帽的少年郎看着往来人群向这里频频侧目，小声提醒。
　　李玄霸仰头，李世民侧头。
　　然后，兄弟二人齐齐脸色一垮，露出了标准的一加一复制粘贴死鱼眼表情▼＿▼。
　　戴着胡帽的少年郎自然是李三娘的未婚夫柴绍。
　　隋朝上层受胡人风俗影响，男女之间相处虽不像盛唐时可以随意杂处，已经订婚的未婚夫妻“偶遇”之后同行一段时间，也是世间允许的。
　　显然，自家三姐早早出门，就是和柴绍约好了“偶遇”。
　　在带他们两个弟弟接收商铺前，这两人大概已经在东市附近的官家园林游玩过了，说不定还去了城郊踏青。
　　李玄霸死鱼眼后，恭敬拱手行礼。
　　李世民则非常不礼貌地瞪了柴绍一眼，然后双手主动死死抱住李三娘的脖子，一副“阿姊是我的，你滚”的态度。
　　李三娘笑着拍了拍二弟的小屁股，道：“你若不喜欢见到他，我就让他走。”
　　柴绍：“？？？”不要啊！他好不容易才为前几日的事哄好了三娘！
　　李世民哼了几声，瓮声瓮气道：“看在他最先冲出去给阿玄找医师的份上，我允许他此次与我们同行。哼，阿姊要嫁给你，以后你和阿姊相处的时间多的是，为何非要霸占我和阿玄与阿姊不多的相处时间？你真讨厌，一点眼色都没有。阿玄所说的没有同理心大概就是指你这样的人。你难道没有即将出嫁的姊妹吗！”
　　收紧手臂，瞪！
　　李三娘藏在冪离下的俊俏小脸笑颜如花。
　　柴绍听了六岁小舅子的埋汰，不仅没生气，还生出了些许好感。
　　李世民前一句话表现出他对待事情很有条理，不会迁怒。后一句话则显示出他对李三娘浓厚的姐弟之情。
　　柴绍是真的心悦李三娘，所以见到李三娘的娘家小兄弟与其感情深厚，心里自然为李三娘高兴。
　　李玄霸叹了一口气，打圆场道：“哥，我和你年幼，阿姊又是未出阁女子。若遇到不长眼的人，需要有个人站在前面挡着。柴兄出现在这里，显然是娘事先定好的。”
　　李世民立刻把嘴嘟得能挂个酒壶：“哼，娘娘不信任我，讨厌！”
　　这时候喊“娘”，和后世叫“妈”一样，有多种变种叫法。如后世的“妈妈、老妈”的撒娇叫法，“娘娘、娘亲”也是撒娇叫法。“娘娘”在从宋朝后，才成为后宫嫔妃与女性神祇的尊称。
　　李世民黏糊糊地撒娇抱怨，还把脑袋埋在李三娘肩膀上碾来碾去。
　　别说李三娘冪离下的笑颜变得越发慈祥，柴绍都看着有些眼热。
　　他本来希望和李三娘多过几年双人生活再求孩子，虽然生孩子这事不以他的希望转移。
　　现在看到李二郎这模样，他觉得如果早早有个李二郎这样的儿子，似乎也不错。
　　反正不能像李三郎。
　　柴绍隐晦地打量李家三郎。
　　李玄霸明明与李世民是双生子，整个人却比李世民小了一圈，因小脸瘦削，居然与李世民看着都不像双生子了。
　　他的儿子如果像李玄霸身体这么弱，那多愁人啊。
　　对了，我儿子该取什么名字？将来要娶哪家的女儿为儿媳？孙儿孙女又该取怎样的名字？若是生了女儿，希望女儿长得像三娘！
　　柴绍思维开始发散，脸上浮现畅想的微笑。
　　李玄霸注意到柴绍在偷偷打量他。他刚反过来打量柴绍，就看见柴绍脸上浮现出典型的陷入幻想的奇怪笑容。
　　略猥琐。
　　李玄霸：“……”对准姐夫的好感度狠狠地下降了。
　　笑闹了一会儿，李三娘终于把李世民放下来，带着两个弟弟去接收母亲赠予的商铺。
　　李玄霸刚进店铺，就让人拿来账本。
　　然后他摸出一本空白的表格账本，李世民从乳母手中接过算盘。
　　李世民翻书、计算、报数，李玄霸捏着羊毫小笔飞速将数字填进表格。
　　柴绍和店铺的掌柜都瞠目结舌。
　　李三娘让掌柜把门帘拉下来，摘掉冪离，颇为自豪地看着两个弟弟忙碌。
　　“三娘子，他们……”柴绍凑到李三娘身边，小声询问。
　　李三娘未等柴绍话说完，就道：“我家二郎三郎最是聪慧，难道你以为李家双生子神童的名声是假的吗？”
　　“你从这家进的香料，吃了一成回扣。”只算完一项买卖，李玄霸就放下笔，平静地对掌柜道。
　　李世民也同时抬头看向掌柜，满脸嘲讽：“娘所说的忠仆，看来很看轻我和阿玄。知道我二人今日要来查账，居然都不把账本改一改吗？”
　　李三娘从袖口拿出那个掌柜的身契扬了扬：“他们的身契都在这里，随二郎和三郎处置。”
　　此时蓄奴合法，店铺里的人自然都是卖身的奴仆。
　　掌柜“扑通”一声跪下，连告饶的声音都发不出来，只不断磕头。
　　李玄霸叹了一口气，道：“罢了，我知道掌管店铺的人都会吃回扣。只吃一成，你算老实了。”
　　李世民抱着手臂冷哼：“只一成还算老实？那我是不是还该感谢他？”
　　李玄霸道：“娘说不定知道这件事，当是给他的辛苦费。潜规则懂吗？要让人给你卖力干活，总要给些甜头。”
　　李世民继续冷哼：“你平时不爱说话，今日话怎么这么多？罢了罢了，既然你这么说，我就不扭送他去见官了。”
　　掌柜一惊一喜，眼泪都冒了出来，连连叩谢两位公子的大恩大德。
　　李三娘全程围观，只偶尔将手中的卖身契扬得哗啦啦响，没插手两个六岁弟弟一唱一和。
　　柴绍的眼神都变了。这两个小舅子，有些太过早熟了吧？
　　或许他不仅要交好未来的唐国公李建成，也得想个办法和这两个孩子拉近关系。
　　李家二郎和三郎就算不能继承爵位，将来也绝非池中物！

Chapter 5: Playing in Tandem to Tame the Shopkeeper

The young masters of the Duke of Tang’s household began their formal education at the age of five, learning literacy, punctuation, and arithmetic.

Once their schooling commenced, they were eligible to receive a monthly allowance.

Li Xuanba had tallied up the pocket money he and his second brother could scrape together each month, and right then and there, the thought of starting a small business took root.

Since he could never achieve glory on the battlefield, amassing some personal wealth before the Sui dynasty descended into chaos seemed wise. That way, when the day came to depend on Li Jiancheng for survival, even if Li Jiancheng despised him, he could still use cold, hard cash to buy his life.

Initially, Li Xuanba assumed that with the Duke of Tang’s estate as his backing, setting up a roadside stall for some petty trade would be effortless.

Only after thorough research did he realize that as a clickbait history writer whose entire livelihood had revolved around plucking Li Shimin’s feathers for web traffic, his grasp of the Sui and Tang dynasties was woefully inadequate.

*Wait. Aren't history marketing accounts just the historically illiterate fleecing the historically illiterate anyway? Ah, never mind then, my professional competence is completely intact.*

How, exactly, did the commercial system of the Sui and Tang operate?

When Emperor Wen of Sui constructed Daxing City, he instituted the strict ward-and-market system to control population movement and suppress commercial enterprise.

A "ward" was a residential district; a "market" was a designated zone for trade. Emperor Wen abolished all street-facing storefronts. Commercial activity was strictly forbidden inside the wards and along the roads connecting them; all transactions had to take place within Daxing's East and West Markets.

Curfews and gate regulations for the wards and markets were ruthlessly enforced. For example, market trading hours: *"In all markets, at midday, three hundred beats of the drum shall assemble the multitude; seven quarters of an hour before sundown, three hundred strikes of the gong shall disperse the multitude."* They were permitted to open for only a single afternoon.

This rigid code was imposed on every city and town across the realm, dictating that *"no market shall be established in any place that is neither a prefectural nor a county seat."*

In the early Sui and Tang dynasties, these rules were draconian. Had Li Xuanba followed his original plan and dragged a small handcart out to sell wares, he would have faced sixty lashes of the cane at best. At worst, both seller and buyer would have been condemned under charges of grand theft.

Just how expansive were these markets where trade was legally permitted?

In the Sui and Tang, the allocation of wards and markets was determined strictly by a city’s administrative rank, irrespective of population size. The capital, Daxing, and the eastern capital, Luoyang, each contained between one hundred and one hundred and ten wards, yet only two markets.

Consequently, the storefronts within these markets could no longer be described merely as "an inch of gold for an inch of land." They were practically priceless, having been carved up completely by the founding nobility and meritorious officials at the Sui dynasty’s dawn.

If Li Xuanba wanted to conduct business covertly inside a residential ward, he would have to wait until the Zhenguan era. Only when his brother realized how thoroughly inconvenient these restrictions were and slightly relaxed control over intra-ward commerce could one dare to set up a stall—and even then, only with powerful backing.

If he wished to rent a roadside building at will and peddle goods through the night, he would have to wait until the An Lushan Rebellion, when the ward-and-market system collapsed altogether.

When Li Xuanba inquired whether his mother would allow him to consign goods through the Duke of Tang's existing family shops and met with a flat refusal, he abandoned all thoughts of entrepreneurship.

A commoner transmigrating to the early or high Tang could forget about launching a small startup stall to strike it rich; even the third young master of the Duke of Tang’s estate couldn't manage it. Alas.

Who would have imagined that merely taking the fall for his eldest brother would yield two prime storefronts?

Though Li Xuanba had mocked his second brother for lacking ambition, his own thought at the time had been: *Damn, this is sweet!*

If not for the fact that he would need to rely on Li Jiancheng for his livelihood later and couldn't afford to push him too far, he would have volunteered to play the victim every single day.

Much like the Chang'an of later years, Daxing City’s imperial detached palaces and aristocratic estates were concentrated near the East Market, formally known as the "Metropolitan Market." The East Market traded primarily in luxuries like gems, antiques, and exquisite silks, and its boulevards were noticeably wider than those of the West Market.

The West Market, dubbed the "Benefiting-the-People Market," catered to commoners. Aside from carrying daily essentials, once the Silk Road reopened in the Zhenguan era, foreign merchants would congregate there in droves. By the High Tang, its bustling prosperity would far outshine the East Market.

At present, though it lacked the boom brought by foreign traders, merchants without noble connections were barred from the East Market, already fostering the dynamic where "the East Market is noble, and the West Market is rich."

Whether in the East or West Market, every shop had long been claimed by the aristocracy. The Sui dynasty had only seen one emperor pass; the nobility was nowhere near the point of political decline that would force them to liquidate their properties.

That Lady Dou and Old Madame Dugu could casually pull out commercial properties for a six-year-old child to "play with" demonstrated the astonishing wealth of their dowries, as well as the towering influence of the Dou and Dugu clans in the Sui court.

Li Xuanba maintained a taciturn demeanor before outsiders, but in Li Shimin’s presence, he was an absolute chatterbox, his thoughts babbling non-stop from the moment they stepped out the door.

Li Shimin leaned against the carriage window, peering outside with wide-eyed curiosity while nodding incessantly to signal that he was listening.

After Li Xuanba meticulously outlined the Sui dynasty’s ward-and-market system, he proceeded to dissect the hidden political undercurrents revealed by their grandmother's and mother's dowries.

Their grandmother’s dowry shops were mostly located in the East Market. In truth, those were not strictly her dowry, but rather imperial rewards bestowed by Empress Wenxian.

Their mother’s shops, on the other hand, lay predominantly in the West Market. This disparity showed that while Emperor Wen of Sui spared the Northern Zhou princesses after annihilating the direct male line of the Yuwen clan, he had still quietly curtailed the influence of Grand Princess Xiangyang’s household.

Li Shimin turned his head. "Is that so? But the shop Grandmother gave you is in the West Market, while Mother’s is in the East Market."

Li Xuanba: [Which proves that while Grandmother and Mother both dote on us, the depth of their affection differs.]

Li Shimin turned back toward the window, resting his chin on his crossed arms and tilting his head thoughtfully. "Ah-Xuan, you said the East Market caters to nobles and the West Market to commoners. Wouldn't that mean shops selling books, paintings, and calligraphy are mostly in the East Market?"

Li Xuanba: [Indeed. The Directorate of Education is located near the East Market, and aspiring scholars seeking officialdom all lodge in the wards surrounding it.]

The Directorate of Education, or Guozixue, was the imperial academy. It would be renamed Guozijian in the third year of the Daye era under Emperor Yang of Sui, reverted to Guozixue in the first year of the Wude era under Gaozu of Tang, and renamed Guozijian once more in the first year of the Zhenguan era under Taizong.

Li Shimin curled his lip. "Then could a bookshop in the West Market even sell anything?"

Li Xuanba: [The West Market is close to Buddhist monasteries. The shop Grandmother gave us mainly sells woodblock-printed Buddhist sutras, so its revenues are actually quite handsome. Grandmother may not spoil us as thoroughly as Mother does, but we are still treasured in her heart.]

Li Shimin settled back beside Li Xuanba and whispered in his ear, "Grandmother's heart must be carved into many slices, and Eldest Brother is definitely the biggest slice."

Li Xuanba choked back a laugh. His second brother’s tongue was razor-sharp; dropped onto the modern internet, he would have been a world-class keyboard warrior.

The shop Lady Dou gifted to Li Xuanba was one of her most lucrative enterprises, the very first property she had managed in her maiden home while learning household administration before marriage. The staff running it were all seasoned retainers brought from her maternal family.

Right beside this property stood the shop Lady Dou had earmarked as part of the dowry for her soon-to-be-wed daughter, Li Sanniang.

For this outing, Lady Dou was occupied attending to Old Madame Dugu, so Li Sanniang had taken charge of bringing her two younger brothers.

This Li Sanniang was none other than the legendary Princess Pingyang Zhao, whom Li Shimin would later grumble about as having "a temper even worse than mine."

In later eras, because Li Shimin ordered the execution of Princess Pingyang Zhao's second son, endless conspiracy theories circulated alleging that he had mistreated her.

Li Xuanba had once written sensationalized clickbait on this very topic, raking in torrential web traffic to fulfill his supervisor’s performance metrics.

Yet to craft a convincing lie, one had to unearth the unvarnished historical truth first—weaving nine parts truth with one part fiction to ensure credibility. Hence, he knew full well the reality was nothing of the sort.

First, Princess Pingyang Zhao had been relieved of all military command as early as the first year of the Wude era, residing quietly in Chang'an ever since.

The name "Niangziguan" (Lady's Pass) had existed centuries before her birth; attributing it to her was merely an embellishment by later romantics.

Having relinquished military power upon the founding of the Tang, she lived in the capital and never garrisoned the pass, making friction between her and the Prince of Qin, Li Shimin—who commanded the empire’s frontline forces—an impossibility.

Furthermore, Li Shimin had treated Princess Pingyang Zhao with extraordinary favor. It was simply that the feudal era's expression of favor toward women failed to align with modern sensibilities.

Before Chai Lingwu and Princess Baling became entangled in treason, Chai Shao’s eldest son had inherited the title of Duke of Qiao, while his second son was ennobled as the Commandery Duke of Xiangyang upon marrying a princess—a rare and glittering lineage boasting two ducal titles under one roof.

Later, although Chai Shao’s eldest son, Chai Zhewei, was implicated in a scandal and exiled to Lingnan, he was swiftly reinstated as Area Commander of Jiaozhou, passing away in office only a year after Li Shimin’s death.

An Area Commander was the supreme local military authority. During the Zhenguan era, domestic commanderies were dismantled, meaning every remaining commander was a powerful frontier governor commanding formidable legions. This stood as clear testament to Li Shimin’s enduring trust.

Li Shimin had likewise extended deep patronage to Princess Pingyang Zhao’s former subordinates, such as the Chai family servant Ma Sanbao.

When Li Yuan raised his banners against the Sui, Chai Shao and Princess Pingyang had acted separately. Chai Shao fled alone to Taiyuan, while Princess Pingyang gathered troops to launch an uprising. Ma Sanbao had stood steadfastly at her side throughout, serving as her most trusted confidant.

In the first year of the Zhenguan era, Ma Sanbao, despite his origins as a household slave, was elevated to the rank of Duke by Li Shimin. When he passed away in the third year of Zhenguan, he was granted the prestigious posthumous title of "Zhong" (Loyal).

Then there was Princess Pingyang Zhao’s husband, Chai Shao, who ranked fourteenth among the Twenty-Four Meritorious Officials of Lingyan Pavilion—ahead of giants like Cheng Yaojin, Hou Junji, and Li Ji.

While Chai Shao had certainly rendered service in defeating the Tuyuhun and the Göktürks, as well as quelling internal rebellions, his military exploits paled in comparison to the other martial legends of the pavilion. His prominent standing was universally acknowledged by posterity as a clear case of "family favoritism."

As for why Princess Pingyang Zhao had not been honored directly in her own right, or why her martial feats were never openly championed, that was simply the tragic limitation of the feudal era.

Feudal honors for women were almost exclusively channeled through their male kin. In lavishing exceptional grace upon her husband, sons, and trusted retainers, Li Shimin was honoring Princess Pingyang Zhao in the only manner the era permitted.

In truth, though the status of women in the Tang dynasty was higher than in the Song and later dynasties, the difference was marginal. In the early Tang, women stepping outdoors were mandated to wear a *mili*—a veil draping over their entire bodies. By the reign of Emperor Gaozong, Li Zhi, when women began wearing *weimao* that only veiled down to the neck, the court issued an imperial edict specifically castigating the trend.

Thus, Princess Pingyang Zhao showing her face in public, recruiting troops, and commanding armies as a female general was profoundly transgressive for her time.

From the Tang’s inception, figures from Li Yuan down to mainstream Confucian scholars worked tirelessly to erase all trace of her martial career.

Immediately after establishing the dynasty, Li Yuan commissioned Wen Daya to pen the *Diary of the Founding of the Great Tang* to extol his own glory. In that chronicle, all of Princess Pingyang Zhao’s deeds were thoroughly expunged, recast as the product of Li Yuan’s unmatched foresight, wisdom, and valor; even her strategic contributions to the capture of Chang'an were credited to his sons and confidants.

In Li Yuan’s own edict commending the conquest, Princess Pingyang Zhao was not mentioned once.

That Li Yuan granted her an official posthumous title and accorded her a funeral complete with martial wind and percussion rites was already an extraordinary concession.

Until the *Old Book of Tang* surfaced centuries later, her brilliance remained thoroughly obscured.

It was against this suffocating social backdrop that Yuchi Yiseng painted a portrait of Princess Pingyang Zhao astride a saddle, equipped with bow and quiver.

The portrait was produced during the Zhenguan era, while Yuchi Yiseng served as Li Shimin’s palace guard. The strings pulled to secure permission for a princess's portrait, and to track down veterans who remembered her days in the field, spoke volumes about the patron behind it.

Li Shimin naturally had every reason to revere this warrior princess and favor her husband and progeny.

According to historical breadcrumbs, Princess Pingyang Zhao’s soldiers had all been incorporated into Li Shimin’s forces, later becoming his most fiercely loyal retainers.

Those men could not have pledged their unyielding allegiance the moment they fell under Li Shimin’s banner simply because he radiated some supernatural charisma that brought men to their knees.

More likely, it validated that old historical appraisal: Princess Pingyang Zhao "was truly difficult to surpass as an elder sister."

Li Xuanba reasoned that even stripped of military command, her former officers would always grant her immense respect. While residing in Chang'an, both Li Yuan and Li Jiancheng would treat this unthreatening yet deeply revered general-princess with the utmost deference.

Thus, he made haste to cling to her coat-tails, ensuring that when the Tang was founded and his brother was away campaigning, he would still have a formidable guardian should he fall out of favor with Li Yuan and Li Jiancheng.

If cornered, he could shamelessly move into his sister’s residence—and quite possibly save her life in the process.

Though historical records were silent on the cause of her death, her second son, Chai Lingwu, was roughly the same age as his wife, Princess Baling, placing his birth right around the time of her passing. Her death had very likely been the result of difficult labor or postpartum complications at an advanced maternal age.

If he made a shameless pest of himself by lodging in the princess’s manor and cockblocking his sister and brother-in-law, perhaps Chai Lingwu would never be conceived, and his sister wouldn't have to die!

A total win-win!

While Li Xuanba’s deliberate pandering had backfired with Li Jiancheng, it had proven overwhelmingly effective with his third sister.

As an unmarried maiden, Li Yuan had not bestowed a childhood courtesy name upon his daughter; she was simply referred to at home and abroad as "Li Sanniang" or "Third Lady."

Li Sanniang had set out earlier than her brothers. By the time their carriage pulled up, she was already standing outside the storefront, draped in a full-body *mili*.

"Er-lang! San-lang!" The spirited Li Sanniang threw open the carriage door before the vehicle had even come to a full stop, scooping both younger brothers into her arms.

Li Xuanba yielded obediently to the embrace.

Li Shimin squirmed violently. "I can walk on my own! Don't carry me!"

Because Li Xuanba was well-behaved, Li Sanniang ruffled his hair affectionately and set him down.

Because Li Shimin was rebellious, she grinned impishly and locked him in a vice-like hold, refusing to let him down no matter how fiercely he flailed.

Li Shimin stretched a hand toward Li Xuanba. "Ah-Xuan, save me!"

Li Xuanba took a step backward, mocking him internally: [Serving as an older sister's toy is a younger brother’s destiny. Accept your fate.]

Li Shimin yelled in frustration, "Then why aren't you her toy!"

Li Sanniang’s laughter rang out like silver chimes. "San-lang says you're my toy? Oh, San-lang, stop whispering to yourself! Sister wants to hear you talk too."

Li Xuanba nodded. "All right."

Li Shimin was positively incensed. "When I tell you to talk, you clamp your mouth shut, but the moment Big Sis asks, you agree?!"

Li Xuanba nodded. "Yes."

Furious, Li Shimin brandished his claws to tackle his brother, but held firm in Li Sanniang’s grasp, he could only flail his short little arms uselessly through the air.

"Ahem, Third Lady, should we head inside first?" A youth wearing a Hu-style hat chimed in softly, noticing the passing pedestrians casting inquisitive glances their way.

Li Xuanba looked up, while Li Shimin turned his head.

Instantly, both brothers’ faces went completely slack, displaying a pair of identical, copy-pasted dead-fish stares ▼＿▼.

The youth in the Hu hat was none other than Li Sanniang’s betrothed, Chai Shao.

Influenced by nomadic customs, the upper crust of the Sui dynasty was not entirely segregated. While young men and women could not mingle with total abandon as they would in the High Tang, it was socially permissible for betrothed couples to "accidentally cross paths" and stroll together for a time.

Clearly, their third sister had set off early today precisely to orchestrate such an "accidental encounter" with Chai Shao.

Before bringing her brothers to inspect the shops, the pair had almost certainly strolled through the imperial gardens near the East Market, or perhaps even enjoyed a spring outing in the city outskirts.

After his dead-fish stare, Li Xuanba politely clasped his hands in formal greeting.

Li Shimin, on the other hand, shot Chai Shao a thoroughly hostile glare, then clamped both arms tightly around Li Sanniang’s neck with an attitude that screamed, *Sister is mine, piss off!*

Li Sanniang chuckled, swatting her second brother’s little bottom. "If you don't like seeing him, I’ll tell him to leave."

Chai Shao: "???" *Please, no! It took mountains of effort to smooth things over with her after the incident the other day!*

Li Shimin gave several indignant snorts, muttering in a sullen voice, "Seeing as he was the first to run out and fetch a physician for Ah-Xuan, I will permit him to accompany us this once. Hmph! Sister is going to marry you anyway, so you’ll have all the time in the world together. Why must you hoard the precious little time Ah-Xuan and I have with her? You are truly tiresome, completely devoid of tact. What Ah-Xuan calls 'lacking empathy' must refer to people like you! Don't you have sisters of your own about to be married off?!"

He tightened his grip on her neck and glared!

Concealed behind her veil, Li Sanniang’s lovely face blossomed into a radiant smile.

Hearing his six-year-old future brother-in-law’s dressing-down, Chai Shao not only felt no offense, but actually experienced a surge of fondness.

Li Shimin’s opening remark proved he was rational and bore no petty grudges, while his second revealed his profound attachment to his sister.

Chai Shao truly adored Li Sanniang, so seeing her younger brothers so deeply devoted to her naturally warmed his heart.

Li Xuanba sighed, stepping in to smooth things over. "Brother, you and I are young, and Sister is an unmarried maiden. If we encounter scoundrels, we need someone to stand in front and shield us. Brother Chai’s presence here was clearly arranged by Mother."

Li Shimin instantly pouted so hard his lips could have held a wine jug. "Hmph! Mother doesn't trust me! How vexing!"

At this time, addressing one’s mother as "Niang" had numerous affectionate variants, much like calling someone "Mom" or "Mama" in later ages; "Niangniang" and "Niangqin" were similarly endearing terms. Only after the Song dynasty would "Niangniang" become an honorific reserved exclusively for imperial consorts and female deities.

Li Shimin whined petulantly, rubbing his head against Li Sanniang’s shoulder.

Not only did Li Sanniang’s smile behind the veil grow increasingly tender, even Chai Shao watched with a pang of envy.

He had originally hoped to enjoy a few years of quiet married life with Li Sanniang before having children—though such matters were hardly up to him.

Seeing Li Er-lang acting so adorably, he thought that having a son like this early on might not be a bad thing after all.

Just so long as he wasn't like Li San-lang.

Chai Shao subtly glanced down at the third son of the Li family.

Though Li Xuanba and Li Shimin were twins, Xuanba was an entire size smaller, his little face gaunt and pale to the point where they scarcely looked related.

If his own son turned out so frail and sickly, what an endless headache that would be.

*Come to think of it, what should I name my son? Which distinguished house's daughter should he take as his bride? And what about our future grandsons and granddaughters? If we have a daughter, I pray she takes after Sanniang!*

Chai Shao’s thoughts began to drift wildly, an idyllic, dazed grin spreading across his face.

Li Xuanba noticed Chai Shao scrutinizing him. Just as he looked back, he caught the older boy wearing an unmistakable, goofy daydreamer’s smile.

It bordered on creepy.

Li Xuanba: "..." His opinion of his future brother-in-law plummeted.

After another round of teasing, Li Sanniang finally set Li Shimin down and ushered her brothers inside to take possession of the shop gifted by their mother.

The moment Li Xuanba stepped through the threshold, he commanded the staff to bring forth the account books.

He then produced a blank, gridded ledger, while Li Shimin accepted an abacus handed over by their wet nurse.

Li Shimin flipped through the pages, calculated, and rattled off figures, while Li Xuanba held a small goat-hair brush, swiftly entering the numbers into the corresponding columns.

Both Chai Shao and the shop’s head manager stood frozen, dumbfounded.

Li Sanniang instructed the manager to lower the entrance curtain, removed her *mili*, and watched her two little brothers at work with immense pride.

"Third Lady, they..." Chai Shao leaned in, whispering hesitantly.

Before he could finish, Li Sanniang cut in, "My Er-lang and San-lang are brilliant beyond measure. Did you truly believe the reputation of the Li family's twin prodigies was a fabrication?"

"You skimmed a ten percent kickback on the spices procured from this merchant," Li Xuanba remarked placidly, laying down his brush after auditing only a single trade.

Li Shimin looked up at the manager at the very same instant, his face dripping with disdain. "It appears the 'loyal servant' Mother spoke of holds Ah-Xuan and me in utter contempt. Knowing we were coming to inspect the books today, you couldn't even be bothered to falsify them beforehand?"

Li Sanniang drew the manager’s indenture contract from her sleeve, giving it a sharp, rustling flick. "Their indentures are all right here, to be dealt with entirely at Er-lang and San-lang’s pleasure."

In this era, owning bondservants was entirely legal; everyone employed in the shop was a bound servant of the estate.

With a heavy *thud*, the manager dropped to his knees. He could not even muster the breath to beg for mercy, able only to knock his forehead repeatedly against the floorboards.

Li Xuanba let out a soft sigh. "Never mind. I am well aware that anyone managing a shop takes a cut. Taking only ten percent means you are relatively honest."

Li Shimin crossed his arms, letting out a frosty sneer. "Only ten percent counts as honest? What, am I supposed to thank him, then?"

Li Xuanba countered, "Mother likely knows of it already and treats it as fair compensation for his toil. Haven't you heard of unspoken rules? If you want people to work themselves to the bone for you, you must throw them a few sweet morsels."

Li Shimin continued his cold scoff. "You're usually a man of few words; why are you blabbering so much today? Fine, fine! Since you put it that way, I won't have him dragged off to the magistrate."

Overcome by shock and relief, tears welled in the manager’s eyes as he kowtowed ceaselessly, showering the two young masters with desperate thanks for their boundless benevolence.

Li Sanniang observed the entire performance, occasionally rustling the contract in her fingers, entirely content not to interrupt her six-year-old brothers' practiced double act.

Chai Shao’s gaze shifted profoundly. Weren't these two little brothers-in-law of his a bit *too* precocious?

Perhaps he needed to do more than just curry favor with the future Duke of Tang, Li Jiancheng—he would have to find a way to forge close ties with these two children as well.

Even if the second and third sons of the Li family were barred from inheriting the ducal title, they were undeniably destined for far greater waters than a shallow pond!

chunks.chapterTitle: 第6章 拉拢阿姊真好哄
chunks.chineseText:
第6章 拉拢阿姊真好哄

吓唬了掌柜，还让掌柜说谢谢后，李玄霸和李世民才继续询问这间铺子的具体情况。
　　李玄霸在心里发言，李世民当外置发声器。
　　虽然李世民掩饰得很好，但和这两个弟弟很熟悉的李三娘，见李世民时不时瞥向李玄霸的幽怨眼神，就知道三郎又偷懒了。
　　二郎和三郎的秘密，只有她和娘最清楚。其余人只知道这对双生子有心灵感应，至于感应到何种程度，他们是不知道的。
　　顶多也就模模糊糊能感受到对方的感情吧？
　　虽然二郎和三郎在家中没怎么掩饰，但这种事，如果他们自己不说清楚，旁的人就算一直听二郎嚷嚷“弟弟开口说话”，也猜不出来具体情况，只以为三郎不爱开口罢了。
　　窦氏让李三娘不要在外面多说二郎和三郎的事。
　　窦氏与李渊不同。
　　李渊因和杨广是表兄弟，很信任杨广。
　　即使李渊的四叔李璋曾在隋文帝杨坚试图篡位时起兵被杀，杨坚看在独孤皇后的份上，都没祸及李渊这一家子，且非常喜爱李渊。
　　李渊没有参与隋文帝暮年诸子夺嫡的斗争。在隋文帝未驾崩时，与隋文帝诸子关系都很融洽。所以他自以为和表弟杨广感情不错。
　　窦氏则因为杨坚杀了他舅舅家所有直系男丁，连禅位的北周静帝都惨遭杀害，对杨家一直很警惕。
　　杨广当太子前后所表现出来的性格作风差异，更让窦氏坚信杨广与杨坚相比，更不是个好相与的。
　　窦氏曾经劝说李渊，“上好鹰爱马，公之所知，此堪进御，不可久留，人或言者，必为身累，愿熟思之”。
　　李渊不听。
　　直到窦氏死了，李渊被杨广打压，才想起窦氏的话，将原先舍不得的鹰犬献给杨广，很快就被拜为将军。这时李渊才思念起窦氏，哭着对儿子们说“我早从汝母之言，居此官久矣”。
　　如今李渊还深信自己很得表弟杨广的宠信，对窦氏隐晦的劝说嗤之以鼻。窦氏只能悄悄自作打算。
　　李三娘很像未出阁的窦氏，虽然才十四岁，心中已经颇有丘壑。
　　柴氏也是高门贵族，柴绍与当今太子杨昭很是亲密。
　　太子杨昭雅性谨重，颇受隋文帝和独孤皇后深爱之，自杨昭出生起，就将其养在膝下。
　　可以说，如今皇帝杨广能成为太子，和隋文帝、独孤皇后喜爱杨昭也有一定关系。
　　杨广继位后，传出弑父的逸闻。
　　杨昭与祖父杨坚感情深厚，且窦氏坚信杨广是个心胸狭隘之人，杨昭在朝堂民间名声都极好，连一直装成明君的杨坚晚年都变得多疑猜忌，杨广将来和太子杨昭必定会有龃龉。柴氏肯定会牵累其中。
　　所以窦氏在李三娘十二岁与柴绍订婚后，就不断提点李三娘。
　　李世民和李玄霸这对双生子祥瑞虽然在外人看来不算什么，也就是多子多福而已。双生子之间有心灵感应，也是自古的记载，算不上多奇特。
　　但谁知道杨广会不会脑袋一拍，就忌惮了。
　　就算一对有奇妙心灵感应的双生子不足以让杨广忌惮唐国公府，那加上太子呢？
　　柴绍与太子杨昭情同手足，李三娘是柴绍之妻，李三娘有一双祥瑞双生子弟弟，这对双生子弟弟还是唐国公府的公子。
　　杨广会不会怀疑，唐国公府用祥瑞双生子给太子造势？
　　窦氏这些怀疑，若李渊听后肯定会嗤之以鼻，但李三娘深信母亲的判断，所以从未对外人提及过两位弟弟真正的奇异之处。
　　李世民和李玄霸也从不会主动提起自己的能力。只是窦氏和李三娘与他们相处久了，自己觉察出来。
　　不过李三娘总认为，不是她们觉察出来，是两个弟弟故意透露给她们。
　　李三娘常和母亲窦氏说，这两个弟弟鬼精鬼精的，真不知道他们小小年纪，为何会如此多的心眼。
　　李玄霸再次偷懒，让二哥当了外置发声器官，安排掌柜稍微更改了一些店铺中的运营策略。
　　刚接手店铺，李玄霸没有做太多改变。
　　做生意和治国一样，不怕循规蹈矩，最怕激进。
　　殊不知许多大企业原本活得好好的，换个二代上来大刀阔斧的改革，几百亿的产值瞬间破产。
　　资本界有个笑话，“不怕二代败家，就怕二代创业”。
　　李玄霸教掌柜用表格记账方式，增加了数字符号和大写数字，然后将潜规则的回扣换成明面上的提成。
　　虽然这样避免不了回扣，但掌柜有了提成拿，就会对销售更上心。
　　吓唬了掌柜一下，掌柜短时间内不敢吃回扣。这段时间，就是李玄霸和李世民将掌柜收为自己人的缓冲时间。
　　待掌柜成为自己人后，李玄霸才会稍稍插手商品贩卖。
　　除了推广表格记账之外，李玄霸只在运营中增加了一项“顾客满意评分”。
　　东市做的大多都是官宦权贵的生意，几乎每一笔买卖都能追溯到某一个具体的权贵家中。李玄霸让掌柜在做成一笔生意之后，就赠送些小礼物，请顾客为此次服务满意度评分，顺带收集顾客的喜好。若评分太低，会扣除部分掌柜的提成。
　　这些将为李玄霸推行会员制做准备。
　　既然是做权贵的奢侈品生意，怎么能没有限量准入的会员制？
　　掌柜已经发现了表格记账的恐怖。
　　虽然表格记账揪出了他的贪婪，但掌柜底下还有伙计，他还要防着伙计的贪婪。在自己暂时不敢伸手的时候，他乐意改个记账方式，让手底下的伙计也不敢伸手。
　　至于服务满意度统计，掌柜没放在心上。
　　这里是大兴城的东市，掉下个竹竿都能砸到几个王公贵族。谁敢对顾客态度不好？
　　询问顾客喜好也是掌柜一直会做的事。
　　若不这么做，他怎么知道接下来进什么货？
　　虽然能凭借销量来判断顾客的喜好，但这会让货品调整慢人一步。赚钱做生意，一步慢就是步步慢。
　　毕竟是连皇帝的行为都能预判的奇女子，窦氏做生意时当然也不会忘了做预测。她经营这个店铺的时候，已经给掌柜打下了良好的习惯。
　　无论是掌柜还是柴绍，都没有听出李世民口中对店铺经营细微调整背后的野心。
　　李三娘听出来了。
　　她眼眸微微一动，但按下了询问的心思。
　　虽然二弟和三弟与她亲近，但将来她会出嫁，还是别多打听。
　　李玄霸注意到李三娘的神色。
　　他放下水杯，对李三娘伸出手，一副累了的模样。
　　李三娘把李玄霸抱到怀里拍了拍：“想睡一会儿吗？”
　　李玄霸压低声音道：“等逛了西市，我和哥有事要和阿姊商量，阿姊记得把柴兄支走一阵子。”
　　李三娘也压低声音道：“为何不直接让他离开？”
　　李玄霸道：“有他在，别人才不知道我们姊弟商议了正事。”
　　李三娘哭笑不得。这个弟弟是不是过于谨慎小心了？只是两间铺子，至于吗？
　　不过弟弟都这么说了，李三娘点头照做。
　　三弟难得的请求，身为阿姊，不能说做不到！
　　李世民说得口干舌燥，回头看见李玄霸正窝在三姐怀里打瞌睡，气得冲过来揪李玄霸的头上的小揪揪。
　　李三娘没有护着李玄霸，任由两个弟弟在她怀里闹腾。
　　虽然她只比两个弟弟大八岁，但现在对待两个弟弟的态度，和母亲没区别。
　　柴绍又看得脸红了，开始畅想他和李三娘子女环绕的场景。
　　李玄霸好不容易把捣乱的哥哥给推开，就看到柴绍那绯红的脸。
　　他再次露出倒三角眼，对准姐夫的好感度再次狠狠地下降。
　　若不是知道历史中柴绍和姐姐的感情极好，即使两人聚少离多，柴绍也除了与姐姐有二子之外再无所出。李玄霸肯定不会阻拦二哥去折腾柴绍。
　　姐姐才十四岁啊，你个十七岁的“大龄少年”别露出这样荡漾的神情，到了现代社会你就是犯罪知道吗！
　　李玄霸也知道自己心中的膈应在这个时代毫无道理，所以就自己腹诽了一下。
　　他非常感谢隋文帝驾崩及时。
　　姐姐十二岁就与柴绍定亲，预定十三岁嫁人。
　　隋文帝去年薨了，母亲和祖母商议后，虽自家只是皇帝的表亲，但仍旧将婚期推迟一年。
　　隋文帝去年七月丁未日去世，但今年七月后没有适合两个孩子的良辰吉日，便把婚期定在明年二月。
　　最初与李三娘亲近，李玄霸是抱有功利的心态。
　　但人的感情都是处出来的，李三娘这性格，与其相处久了谁能不动真心？
　　李玄霸表面上装得很淡然，实际上对三姐早早出嫁很是不愿意。他只能安慰自己，十五岁出嫁总比十三岁出嫁好。
　　感谢隋文帝！
　　李玄霸正走神，李世民一个猛扑，不小心把弟弟从李三娘怀里推了下来。
　　在李玄霸被推下来的时候，李世民吓了一跳，赶紧把李玄霸一拉。
　　李玄霸倒下时换了个方向，把李世民垫在了地上。
　　“哎哟。”李世民护着弟弟哀嚎。
　　李玄霸从李世民身上爬下来，骂道：“活该。”
　　“嘿嘿。”李世民揉了揉屁股装傻，笑着混过去。
　　李三娘和柴绍都忍俊不禁。连管家都有些抑制不住嘴角上扬。
　　刚刚两位公子还早熟得吓人，现在恢复了孩童的模样，管家心中对“神童”产生的不适和恐惧都消散了。
　　东市的店铺很好收服，西市就麻烦了些。
　　打狗也要看主人。“孝”字当头，就是长辈身边的奴仆，晚辈都得给几分薄面。
　　李玄霸在心里阴阳怪气：【不然他们就会告状，‘他这是在打我的屁股吗！这是在打您的脸！’】
　　这时还没有“您”这个字，但李世民也听出了李玄霸的阴阳怪气。
　　他凑到李玄霸耳边道：“奴仆的屁股是主家的脸，这骂谁啊？”
　　李玄霸还没回答，李世民就捧腹大笑，东倒西歪。
　　柴绍见李家二郎好端端地突然笑起来，满头雾水。
　　李三娘则心里发痒。
　　不知道三郎又和二郎说了什么笑话，把二郎乐成这样。唉，要是柴绍不在身边就好了。
　　自己的武力足以保护幼弟，但偏偏不能在外人面前舞刀弄枪，与人争执，真烦。
　　西市的掌柜仗着自己辈分高，比东市的掌柜更棘手几分。
　　李玄霸和李世民遵循“不能打祖母的脸”的前提，改变了策略。
　　他们照旧算账，照旧指出掌柜吃了回扣。
　　啧啧啧，足足四成回扣。原来印刷佛经贩卖利润这么高？
　　这次李玄霸和李世民你唱我和换了个剧本。
　　李世民只一眨眼，眼睛里就泛出气愤的泪水，说要向祖母告状，把偷祖母钱的掌柜送官府。
　　李玄霸哭不出来，只能装得一副唯唯诺诺犹犹豫豫的模样，说担心祖母脸面上不好看，反正祖母已经把掌柜的卖身契给了他们，就他们自己偷偷解决。
　　李世民哭闹，我不听我不听，我一定要向祖母告状。
　　李玄霸继续手足无措，也嘴一瘪，一副要哭不哭的模样。
　　李世民见弟弟那别扭的表情，好不容易从心底挤出一个字嘲笑弟弟：【哈！】
　　李玄霸在心底咬牙切齿：【你‘哈’什么！】
　　李世民在心底努力一个字一个字地蹦：【哈！】【装！】【哭！】【不！】【像！】
　　终于努力把这几个字蹦完，李世民往弟弟身上一倒，有气无力道：“累，头晕。”
　　李玄霸接住磅重的哥哥：【你精神力没我强，就不要用心声对我说话。】
　　李世民靠着弟弟偷偷打了个哈欠，装作哭累的模样继续抽泣。
　　李三娘适时加入这场闹剧，先命带来的家丁把掌柜控制住，并派人去如实禀报祖母，告诉祖母自己先带着哭闹不止的二郎和三郎去玩一会儿，把两个弟弟逗开心了再回来亲自禀报。
　　这时充当背景板的柴绍终于起了作用。
　　他见掌柜污言秽语不断，按着掌柜的后脑勺，将掌柜的脸砸在了地上，砸得掌柜门牙断了半截，满口鲜血哀嚎不已。
　　“把他嘴堵住，别污了贵人的耳。”柴绍对自己的家丁命令道。
　　李世民赶紧伸手死死捂住李玄霸的眼睛。他自己倒是毫不害怕，还颇为好奇地打量这位出手果断的姐夫。
　　李玄霸无语。
　　自己也不害怕好吗？和二哥说了很多次，他、不、怕！
　　但二哥每次见到有人斗殴或者有下人被责罚，都会不记得他的话，非要捂住他的眼睛，搞得祖母和母亲都以为他胆小。
　　李三娘眼睛一亮。三郎要的机会，这不就来了吗？
　　李三娘假装皱起眉头，对柴绍道：“柴郎，我带二郎和三郎在一旁饮子铺坐坐，你处理完这里的事后，给二郎和三郎买点糕点再来寻我。”
　　柴绍立刻满脸堆笑答应。
　　李世民刚对柴绍生出的好感，瞬间狠狠下降。
　　啧，笑得好谄媚，好难看。
　　刚把二哥的挡住自己眼睛的手扯下来的李玄霸也分外无语。
　　自家母亲给阿姊挑的夫婿，长相肯定是不差的。但柴绍柴大郎君，你是不是该做一做表情管理训练？白瞎了你那张俊脸。
　　看看我哥，就是嚎啕大哭都哭得那么好看，放后世一定能当个巨红童星。
　　李三娘倒是不嫌弃柴绍突然崩掉的颜值，又叮嘱了柴绍几句后，带着李玄霸和李世民离开书店，去了不远处的饮子铺。
　　此时的茶还是加了许多奇怪佐料的茶汤，虽已经有茶摊，但茶汤还是多在食肆贩卖。直到开元年间，才有单独的茶肆茶馆雏形出现。
　　如今的“饮料店”叫饮子铺，是用各种花草、果脯熬制的类似于后世花草茶、凉茶之类的饮品。
　　饮子铺一般都和药铺是一个东家，主卖的“特色饮子”都会有医师冠名认证，不说包治百病，至少也会有一二保健养生的疗效。
　　李三娘在二楼选了个僻静的带屏风和盆栽格挡的角落。她又以喜欢清净的借口，买下了附近几桌的空位，与其他客人隔出一圈空间，并给带来的家丁买了饮子，让家丁在空圈外又围了一圈坐着休息。
　　“好了，三郎，有什么要和阿姊说的？”李三娘问道。
　　李世民从怀里摸出一卷纸递给李三娘，抱怨道：“稍稍重一点的东西，阿玄就爱往我怀里塞。”
　　李玄霸捧着只放了梅干和甘草的饮子不说话。
　　大热天的，他才不想在怀里塞太多东西，会掉出来。
　　李三娘把李世民塞过来的纸展开，只看了几行就惊讶道：“你要和我一同做生意？”
　　李玄霸点头，正准备让二哥继续给自己当传声筒，李世民双臂在胸前交叉表示拒绝：“你自己和阿姊说，哥哥累了。”
　　说完，他就捧着饮子埋头牛饮，无论李玄霸怎么在心里戳他，他都不理睬。
　　李玄霸见外置发声器官罢工，只能劳累自己开口。
　　“以后我会弄出一些新鲜玩意儿出来贩卖。孩童过于聪慧会被认为是妖异。当朝皇帝不是个心胸宽广的人，我和二哥过于突出，恐怕会引起他的不满……”
　　李玄霸话未说完，李世民抬起头道：“你何必对阿姊遮掩？不如直说我俩头上有个袭爵的兄长，我俩过于出色，可能会引发兄长妒忌。哼，我多在祖母怀里腻一会儿，兄长的眼神就和下刀子似的，小气。”
　　李玄霸没好气道：“你不是不累吗？帮我说。”
　　李世民立刻低头继续捧着瓷杯装作喝水：“现在累了。”
　　李三娘忍着笑道：“好了，我知道了，确实有这个问题。你们上头有袭爵的兄长，在兄长有实职前，还是低调些好。”
　　虽然现在他们的父亲李渊身体还硬朗，离李建成袭爵还早。但等李建成成婚后，父亲肯定会为李建成谋求实职。
　　一般而言，这实职都是入宫廷或东宫为侍卫官，如柴绍目前的“左千牛备身”。
　　柴绍因与太子杨昭关系莫逆，刚与李三娘订婚就成了左千牛备身，专职保护太子。
　　千牛备身是隶属于千牛卫的禁卫武官，能执“千牛刀”入禁中，常备皇帝和太子身边。换作后世熟悉的称呼，叫“御前带刀侍卫”。
　　隋唐禁军分南北衙门。南衙统领天下府兵，北衙是皇帝私人募兵。
　　在府兵制崩坏前，千牛卫就是禁军的核心，也是勋贵青年武将培养基地。
　　这时男子也是普遍及冠后才担任实职，李建成就在等冠礼后李渊帮他寻个实职。
　　如柴绍这样还未成婚，就已经是左千牛备身，在禁中持刀保卫太子安全，可谓是少年英才，前途无量。
　　窦氏深知自家女儿内心的骄傲，若所嫁之人空有家世，自己没什么本事，女儿是很难与其有感情的，选女婿时费了很多心思。
　　李建成还未及冠，身上没有实职，才会盯着后院兄弟。待李建成有了实职后，他就会着眼朝堂，看不上后院那一亩三分地，也就不会再和小他十岁的两个弟弟置气了。
　　“再者，我见其他世族大家，偏房行商供主房入仕用钱，却常常不得尊重，所赚取钱财被主房任意支取，影响买卖。若我和哥哥的铺子有阿姊一份投入，想来将来唐国公府是不好意思去任意支取外嫁女儿铺子里的钱的。”
　　李玄霸委婉道：“不是我不信父亲和兄长品行，只是我身体过于病弱，恐怕将来难以在仕途上有所成就，只能混些钱财傍身。让阿姊见笑了。”
　　李世民再次插嘴：“我和阿玄还年幼，祖母和母亲就叮嘱我和阿玄要讨好兄长，以免兄长将来当了家对我们不好。那我和阿玄就不靠唐国公府，靠阿姊了。阿姊以后是钜鹿郡公家的当家主母，也能护得住我和阿玄。”
　　李三娘哭笑不得：“二郎，三郎，你们信任阿姊，阿姊很高兴。但阿姊外嫁后就是柴家妇，你们怎么能更信外人？”
　　李世民摇头：“我不信什么内人外人。我信阿姊，不信兄长。”
　　李玄霸瞥了二哥一眼。
　　他本来想说，“阿姊出嫁了也是阿姊，不是外人”。没想到二哥先插嘴，而这插嘴的话，似乎比自己所说的更高明。
　　看看阿姊瞬间绽放的笑容和明亮的眸子，二哥不愧是二哥，这张嘴太会说了。
　　“既然你们都这么说了，阿姊向你们承诺，阿姊用嫁妆陪你们做生意，不会让柴家人插手。”李三娘被二弟三弟如此信任，心中不由生出了一股豪情。
　　咳，她倒不是认为父亲和兄长真的会贪图两个孩童手中的零花钱，只是陪弟弟玩耍而已。
　　李世民和李玄霸交换了一个眼色。
　　搞定！
　　阿姊真好哄！
